unit.title: Use online systems to support managerial decision- making

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A sales manager in Kingston must decide whether to open late on Fridays. Before logging in to any system, what should she do first?
options: Download every report the system offers
Ask IT to buy a new reporting tool
Pick the answer first, then look for support
Define the decision and the data she needs

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What term describes data that is updated the moment a transaction happens?
What term names the work of finding and correcting errors, duplicates and gaps in a data set before it is analysed?
What name is given to the time-stamped log of each user's actions in a system, used to check who did what?
What word names a fake email or message that tries to trick a person into giving away passwords or other details?
A call centre's target is 1,200 calls answered a day. Today 1,050 were answered. What percentage of the target was reached?
A project has a 40% chance of earning J$3,000,000 and a 60% chance of earning nothing. What is its expected value, in J$?
An online report shows 45 late deliveries out of 900 deliveries. What percentage was late?
What word names the type of analytics that explains why something happened, for example why sales fell in one branch?
What term names a login method that needs a password plus a second check, such as a code sent to a phone?
What word names a copy of data kept separately so that it can be restored if the original is lost?
What term describes the rule that each person can open only the data that their job requires?
What two-word term names a diagram of possible choices, their chances and their outcomes, used to work out expected values?
What two-word term names the share of website visitors who leave after viewing only one page?
What two-word term names data sets so large and fast-growing, such as every till transaction in a supermarket chain, that ordinary tools cannot handle them?
What term names the storing and running of software and data on remote servers reached over the internet?

essays.stem: Explain how online systems can support each stage of a manager's decision-making process, using an example from a retail or hospitality business.
essays.modelAnswer: Take a restaurant manager in Ocho Rios deciding whether to add a lunch delivery service. In the first stage, defining the problem, the point-of-sale system's reports show that lunchtime dine-in sales have fallen for six months, which frames the decision. In the second stage, gathering information, she uses the sales system for trends by day and dish, an online customer survey to ask whether people would order delivery, and online research on delivery costs and local competitors. In the third stage, developing and weighing options, she builds a shared spreadsheet comparing delivery through her own driver, a delivery partner or no change, with costs, expected orders and risks, and invites her assistant managers to comment online. In the fourth stage, choosing, she uses these figures and her own judgement to select an option, and records her reasons in the shared file. In the fifth stage, carrying out the decision, online tools such as a booking or ordering page and staff messaging support the roll-out. Finally, in the review stage, the dashboard tracks delivery orders, profit and customer ratings against the targets she set.
markingPoints: Uses a clear business example throughout
Shows how systems help define the problem
Shows how systems help gather information and weigh options
Shows how systems support choosing, recording and acting
Shows how systems support review against targets

essays.stem: Design a management dashboard for the general manager of a 60-room hotel in Ocho Rios. Explain which measures you would include, why, and how the dashboard would be used.
essays.modelAnswer: The dashboard would show a small number of measures linked to the hotel's main goals, on one screen, updated daily from the booking, sales, accounts and guest feedback systems. For revenue, it would show the occupancy rate, the average room rate and revenue per available room, each against the budget and last year, because these drive the hotel's income. For costs, it would show payroll as a share of revenue and food cost in the restaurant, because these are the largest costs the manager can control. For guests, it would show the online review score and the number of complaints, because reputation drives future bookings. For staff, it would show absence and overtime hours. Each measure would use a simple chart or a red, amber and green colour to show whether it is on target, and the manager could click on any figure to see more detail, such as occupancy by room type. The manager would review the dashboard each morning, set alerts for large changes, discuss it with department heads at a weekly meeting, and use it to decide actions such as special offers or roster changes.
markingPoints: Measures are few and linked to key goals
Includes revenue or occupancy measures with reasons
Includes cost, guest and staff measures with reasons
Describes layout: targets, colours, charts, drill-down and data sources
Explains how it is used for regular review and decisions

essays.stem: A supermarket chain is deciding how to launch online ordering with home delivery. An online survey was sent to 1,200 customers; 480 replied, and 300 of those said they would use the service. Option 1, an island-wide launch, has a 50% chance of a J$6,000,000 profit and a 50% chance of a J$2,000,000 loss in the first year. Option 2, a launch in Kingston only, has a 70% chance of a J$3,000,000 profit and a 30% chance of a J$500,000 loss. Work out the survey response rate, the share of respondents who would use the service, and the expected value of each option. Then make a recommendation.
essays.modelAnswer: The response rate is 480 out of 1,200, which is 40%. Of those who replied, 300 out of 480, or 62.5%, said they would use the service, which is encouraging, although people who replied may be keener than those who did not, so actual use may be lower. The expected value of Option 1 is 50% of J$6,000,000, which is J$3,000,000, minus 50% of J$2,000,000, which is J$1,000,000, giving J$2,000,000. The expected value of Option 2 is 70% of J$3,000,000, which is J$2,100,000, minus 30% of J$500,000, which is J$150,000, giving J$1,950,000. The expected values are very close, only J$50,000 apart, but the risks are very different: Option 1 has an even chance of losing J$2,000,000, while Option 2's worst result is a loss of J$500,000. I would recommend Option 2. Launching in Kingston first carries far less risk for almost the same expected value, and the chain can use the online system's data on orders, delivery times and customer ratings to improve the service before extending it island-wide.
markingPoints: Response rate of 40% and 62.5% would use
Option 1 expected value of J$2,000,000
Option 2 expected value of J$1,950,000
Compares risk, not only expected value, and notes survey bias
Makes a justified recommendation

essays.stem: Explain what makes data good enough to base a management decision on, and describe how a manager can check the quality of data drawn from an online system.
essays.modelAnswer: Good data for decisions is accurate, meaning it records what really happened; complete, with no missing branches, days or types of transaction; timely, meaning recent enough for the decision; consistent, so that the same item is measured the same way in every place and period; and relevant to the question being asked. It should also come from a trusted source and be secure from tampering. A manager can check accuracy by comparing a sample of system figures with the source documents, such as till receipts or delivery notes, and by looking for odd values, such as one day's sales ten times higher than usual, which often show an entry error. She can check completeness by confirming that every branch and period is included and that totals match other reports, such as the accounts. She should note the date each report was last updated. She can check consistency by making sure that definitions, such as what counts as a complaint, are the same across branches. Problems should be reported to the system owner and corrected, and the manager should be open about any limits that remain when she presents her decision.
markingPoints: Names accuracy, completeness and timeliness
Names consistency, relevance or reliability of the source
Checks samples against source documents and looks for odd values
Checks totals, dates and definitions
Reports and corrects problems and states limits

essays.stem: Explain the security and data protection risks of using online systems for management decisions, and describe the controls a manager should insist on.
essays.modelAnswer: Online systems hold valuable data, such as sales, prices, staff records and customers' personal details, so they attract attack and misuse. The main risks are stolen or weak passwords, phishing emails that trick staff into giving access, staff seeing or changing data they should not, data lost through system failure or ransomware, and personal data being copied to personal phones or sent to the wrong person. Any of these can lead to poor decisions based on altered data, financial loss, harm to customers and a breach of the data protection law. A manager should insist on strong passwords and two-factor login for every user, and on access rights set by role so that each person sees only what their job needs. Accounts of staff who leave should be closed at once. Systems should log who views and changes data. Data should be backed up regularly and restores tested. Staff should be trained to spot phishing and to report incidents quickly. Personal data should be collected only for a clear purpose, kept on approved systems, not on personal devices, and deleted when no longer needed.
markingPoints: Identifies password, phishing and access risks
Identifies data loss and personal data risks and their effects
Requires strong passwords, two-factor login and role-based access
Requires logging, backups and prompt closing of leavers' accounts
Requires staff training and handling of personal data under the law

essays.stem: Compare descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics, and give an example of how a manager might use each.
essays.modelAnswer: Descriptive analytics tells a manager what has happened, by summarising past data in reports and charts. For example, a courier firm's manager looks at a report of deliveries completed by each route last month. Diagnostic analytics asks why something happened, by drilling down into data and comparing groups. The same manager might find that late deliveries rose because one route had several new drivers and road works. Predictive analytics uses past patterns to estimate what is likely to happen, such as forecasting how many parcels will arrive in the busy pre-Christmas weeks, so that extra drivers can be hired in time. Prescriptive analytics goes a step further and suggests what to do, for example a routing tool that recommends the best order of stops for each van to save time and fuel. The four types build on each other: descriptive and diagnostic look back, while predictive and prescriptive look forward and need more data and more advanced tools. The more advanced the tool, the more important it is for the manager to check its assumptions and use her own judgement before acting.
markingPoints: Explains descriptive analytics with an example
Explains diagnostic analytics with an example
Explains predictive analytics with an example
Explains prescriptive analytics with an example
Compares them and notes the need for judgement

essays.stem: A hardware company is deciding whether to open a new branch in May Pen. Explain how a manager should use online research to support the decision, and how she should judge the reliability of what she finds.
essays.modelAnswer: The manager should first list the questions the research must answer, such as the size and growth of the local population, building and farming activity in the area, competitors already there, the cost of renting premises, and the availability of staff. She can then search official sources, such as national statistics on population and the economy, the parish municipal corporation's information on planning and building approvals, and the companies registry to check competitors. Property firms' websites can give rents, and online maps can show traffic, access and nearby businesses. Competitors' websites and social media show their range and prices, and customer reviews give clues about gaps in service. She should judge each source by who produced it, whether they are expert and independent, how recent the information is and how it was collected. Official and reputable professional sources usually deserve more weight than anonymous posts or advertisements. Where possible, she should confirm important figures from more than one source, and record each source and date. Online research should be combined with a site visit and talks with local people before the final decision.
markingPoints: Defines the questions the research must answer
Uses suitable official and commercial online sources
Uses competitor and customer information
Judges reliability by author, independence, date and method
Cross-checks, records sources and combines with other evidence

essays.stem: Managers at three branches must make a joint decision about a new staff roster. Explain how online collaboration tools can support the decision, and the risks they must manage.
essays.modelAnswer: Online collaboration tools let the managers work together without travelling. A shared folder can hold the information everyone needs, such as current rosters, sales by hour and staff availability, so that all three see the same figures. A shared spreadsheet can hold the draft roster, with each manager adding comments and suggested changes, and version history shows who changed what and lets the group return to an earlier version if needed. A short video meeting can be used to discuss the options, with the screen shared so that everyone looks at the same draft. An online poll can help the group choose between options, and the final decision and reasons can be recorded in the shared folder. The risks include people editing separate copies so that versions conflict, which is avoided by keeping one master file. Access must be limited to those who need it, because rosters contain personal details, and files should not be shared through personal accounts. Some managers may have weak internet or limited skills, so training and a back-up plan are needed. The group should also agree deadlines and who makes the final decision.
markingPoints: Shared storage so all use the same information
Shared documents with comments and version history
Video meetings and polls to discuss and decide, with a record kept
Manages version conflict and access to personal data
Manages skills, connectivity and decision roles

essays.stem: Explain the risks of relying too heavily on online system outputs when making decisions, and how a manager can balance data with judgement.
essays.modelAnswer: Online systems can make figures look precise and certain, but they are only as good as the data and rules behind them. If data is wrong, incomplete or out of date, the output will mislead. Systems measure what can be counted, such as sales and costs, and may miss things that matter, such as staff morale, a competitor's plans or a customer's loyalty. Recommendations from automated tools rest on assumptions that may no longer hold, for example a forecast based on years before a hurricane or a new road. Managers can also fall into confirmation bias, looking only for figures that support what they already want, or suffer information overload when there are too many reports to make sense of. To balance data with judgement, the manager should be clear about the decision and the few measures that matter, check the quality and age of the data, and ask what the figures do not show. She should talk to staff and customers, consider her own experience, and test the decision against more than one source. Important decisions should be reviewed by a colleague, and their results tracked afterwards.
markingPoints: Risk of poor-quality or out-of-date data
Risk of missing factors that cannot be counted
Risk of hidden assumptions, bias or overload
Balances data with experience, staff and customer views
Checks, reviews and tracks results

essays.stem: Describe how you would design and use an online customer survey to help decide whether a pharmacy chain should change its opening hours, and how you would analyse the results.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start by stating the decision and the information needed: which hours customers want, how often they would use extended hours and at which branches. The survey would be short, about eight questions, so that people finish it. Questions would be clear and neutral, mostly closed, such as asking customers to choose their preferred closing time from a list, with one open question for comments. I would include a question on the branch they use, but avoid collecting names or other personal details unless necessary, and state how the data will be used, in line with the data protection law. I would test the survey on a few colleagues first to remove confusing questions. To reach a fair sample, I would share the link by text message, email, social media and a QR code at the till, and run it for two weeks, offering a paper version for customers who do not use the internet. To analyse the results, I would work out the response rate, then the percentage choosing each option, by branch, and summarise the comments into themes. I would compare the results with till data on busy hours before recommending a decision.
markingPoints: Starts from the decision and the information needed
Short, clear, neutral questions, tested first
Protects personal data and explains its use
Reaches a fair sample through several channels
Analyses response rate, percentages by group and themes, and cross-checks with other data

practical1.title: Build a dashboard from online data and use it to make and justify a decision
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a data file for a made-up business (for example twelve months of sales, costs, staff hours and customer ratings for a chain of four pharmacies, or bookings and revenue for a guest house group) and a decision to make, such as which branch should open on Sundays. Using the Centre's spreadsheet or online spreadsheet tool, produce: a data quality log listing the errors, gaps and odd values found and how each was handled; a one-screen dashboard with no more than six key measures, each against a target, with charts and a filter by branch or month; a drill-down sheet showing the detail behind the most important change; a comparison of the options with the figures worked out and checked twice (for example the expected value of each option, or the profit each would bring); and a one-page decision memo giving the decision, the evidence, its limits and how the result will be reviewed. Give each member a named role: data quality checker, dashboard builder, analyst (drill-down and option figures), decision writer, and presenter (explains the dashboard and memo to the assessor). In a group of four, the analyst also presents. Take a screenshot at each stage.
materials: Data file and decision card from the assessor
Computers with spreadsheet software or an online spreadsheet tool on a Centre account
A screen or projector for presenting
photos: The dashboard on screen with targets and charts
The filter in use, showing one branch or month
The option comparison with its figures
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Errors and gaps in the data were found and handled sensibly
The dashboard shows a few relevant measures against targets and is easy to read
The decision follows from the evidence and states its limits
The review plan names measures and a date
Explained their part clearly to the assessor
safety: Use only the made-up data file; enter no real customer or staff data
Save work only to the Centre's computers or Centre account, not to personal devices
Log out of any online tool at the end of the session
Take regular screen breaks and share the work fairly

practical2.title: Design and run an online survey, analyse the results and present a recommendation
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a decision for a made-up business (for example whether a gym in Portmore should open at 5 a.m., or which new menu items a café in Mandeville should add). Using the Centre's online form tool on a Centre account, your group designs, tests and runs a short anonymous survey, sent to trainees in other groups who agree to take part, then analyses the results and presents a recommendation. Produce: a survey plan stating the decision, the information needed and the target respondents; the survey of six to ten clear, neutral questions, with a short note at the start explaining its purpose and that no names are collected; a record of the test run and the changes made; the results exported into a spreadsheet, with the response rate and the percentage for each answer worked out and checked twice, and at least two charts; and five slides presenting the findings, their limits and the recommendation. Give each member a named role: survey designer, tester (runs the test with two people and records changes), data protection lead (writes the purpose note and checks no personal data is collected), analyst (spreadsheet and charts), and presenter. In a group of four, the tester also acts as data protection lead. Every member presents part of the findings.
materials: Centre computers with internet access, the online form tool and a Centre account set up by the assessor
photos: The survey on screen, showing the purpose note and the questions
The test-run record with the changes made
The results spreadsheet with the response rate and percentages
The presentation with the slides showing
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Questions are clear, neutral and linked to the decision
No personal data is collected and the purpose is explained
The response rate and percentages are correct
Charts are suitable and clearly labelled
The recommendation follows from the results and notes their limits
safety: Collect no names, phone numbers or other personal details
Ask only trainees who agree to take part, and let anyone decline
Use only the Centre account and delete the survey and responses after assessment if the assessor asks
